title: The daily banis, in the code
hook: the code lists the morning, evening and night banis

segments.voice: Yesterday, who is a Sikh: the code's answer, one God, the ten Gurus, the Granth, their teachings and the Tenth Guru's amrit. Your line was belief, plainly put. What did your plain lines say? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

On an old sailing ship, a bell was struck at set times through the day and the night, so everyone aboard knew where the day stood without looking for a clock. The day had marks in it, and the marks held the crew together. Yesterday the code told us who a Sikh is. Today it gives the Sikh day its marks: which prayers are said, and when. It names them by the hour: morning, evening, night.
screen: `A BELL AT SET HOURS.` → `THE DAY HAS MARKS IN IT.` → `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The daily set is called nitnem, the daily rule. Each piece in it is a bani, a composition of the Gurus. In paraphrase, here is what the code lists. In the morning: Japji Sahib, the Jaap Sahib, and the Ten Swayyas, the ones that begin with the words sravag sudh. In the evening: Sodar Rehras, a gathering of hymns read as the day goes down. At night, before sleep: Sohila. We touched part of this list a few days ago, from the Tenth Guru's side. Now look at all of it, and at who is speaking. Japji Sahib is Guru Nanak's, the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib. The Jaap Sahib and the Swayyas are the Tenth Guru's, the writings we have spent the last weeks with. So the morning opens with the first Guru and the Tenth side by side, the beginning of the line and its end, before breakfast. Then look at the shape. Three doors in the day. One as it starts, one as it turns toward dark, one as it closes. Nobody has to decide each day whether to pray or what to say. The code has already set the table. One caution. The code's list is a shared floor, not a ceiling. Some Sikh communities and schools add more banis to the morning, and families keep their own additions. The code names what Sikhs agree on together. And this is where the week turns. It began with the Tenth Guru's own writings, praise and rebuke and song. It ends with two of those same writings set into a daily timetable, so that the Guru's words aren't only studied. They're said aloud, morning after morning.
screen: `NITNEM: THE DAILY RULE.` · `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.` · `THE FIRST GURU AND THE TENTH TOGETHER.` · `A SHARED FLOOR, NOT A CEILING.` · then, large: `THE CODE'S NITNEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: review your own daily rhythm. Settle, and breathe. Walk through yesterday in your mind: waking, midday, evening, the moment before sleep. Where were the doors? A moment of quiet, a word of thanks, a prayer, or nothing at all. Don't judge it; just see it. Then choose one of those doors and picture what you'd like to find there. If you pray, you can rest on the name Waheguru with each breath. The bell holds the time.
The daily banis. The code's nitnem: Japji, Jaap and the Swayyas at morning, Rehras at evening, Sohila at night. Today's word.
Your line: the code's nitnem. Today, mark the three doors of your own day, morning, evening and night, and stop at each one for a single breath. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep nitnem recite the morning banis after waking, Rehras in the evening and Sohila before sleep, often from a gutka or from memory; some communities add further banis to the morning.

notes: The code's nitnem is paraphrased: morning, Japji Sahib, Jaap Sahib and the Ten Swayyas beginning 'sravag sudh'; evening, Sodar Rehras; night, Sohila. Please confirm the list and the naming ('Ten Swayyas' is the code's own name for that set).
'Some Sikh communities and schools add more banis to the morning' (e.g. Chaupai, Anand Sahib) is stated without naming which; please confirm the framing is fair to all sides.
Japji Sahib is described as the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib (Ang 1); please confirm phrasing given the Mool Mantar opens it.
